sentences.text: In 2024, the index leans most toward China in Suriname (+38), Peru (+34) and Bolivia (+31) and least in Paraguay (+0) and Argentina (-13) (net lean, China minus the United States, in index points); 10 of the twelve countries have an index that year.
No index for Uruguay and Venezuela in 2024: fewer than three components are available (no reported trade, or sources that end earlier).
Between 2019 and 2024 the Chinese index rose most in Brazil (+10.2) and Bolivia (+9.6) and fell most in Suriname (-13.2) and Argentina (-7.3).

Across the reporting countries in 2025, the minerals whose exports go most to China are lithium (73%), iron ore (68%) and manganese (62%); those going most to the United States are tin (17%), bauxite aluminum (14%) and copper (13%) (minerals with at least US$100 m of exports).
A Herfindahl index of destinations is not computed: the warehouse holds partner totals for the United States, China and the world only.

Documented commitments to the twelve countries total US$195.1 bn from Chinese institutions over 2000–2021 (858 events) and US$6.0 bn from US institutions over 1986–2024 (84 events); swap-line drawdowns are excluded and the two sources end in different years (see the caveats).

The most connected lenders in the finance network are China Development Bank (CDB) (161 recipients), Unspecified Chinese Government Institution (125 recipients), China Ministry of Commerce (90 recipients) and Export-Import Bank of China (China Eximbank) (90 recipients).

In the panel regressions, the share of exports going to China moves -1.2 points per standard deviation of finance flow lag1 (cluster p 0.11, wild bootstrap p 0.04; dropping one country at a time keeps it between -1.7 points and -0.5 points); an association with country and year effects, not a causal estimate.

In the panel regressions, the share of imports coming from the United States moves +15.7 points per standard deviation of electoral democracy (cluster p <0.01, wild bootstrap p 0.03; dropping one country at a time keeps it between +9.5 points and +17.7 points); an association with country and year effects, not a causal estimate.

The event windows least like the rest of their own series are Argentina after Argentina: Ley 27.742 (Ley Bases) promulgated, creating the RIGI large-investment regime used by lithium and copper projects (2024), where the share of exports to China moved +15.0 points (placebo p 0.07), Chile after China: export controls on antimony items in force (Announcement 2024 No. 33 of 15 August 2024) (2024), where the share of exports to the United States moved +4.9 points (placebo p 0.07) and Argentina after China: export controls on antimony items in force (Announcement 2024 No. 33 of 15 August 2024) (2024), where the share of exports to China moved +15.0 points (placebo p 0.07); the event list is still in draft.

For the influence index toward the United States, the published model is damped local linear trend (Kalman filter, maximum likelihood): CRPS 4.73 against 5.09 for naive persistence over 246 backtest cases, with 80% bands covering 77% of outcomes.

For the influence index toward China, the published model is naive persistence (last value; bootstrapped yearly changes): CRPS 3.94 against 3.94 for naive persistence over 243 backtest cases, with 80% bands covering 73% of outcomes.

For the export share toward the United States, the published model is naive persistence (last value; bootstrapped yearly changes): CRPS 4.39 points against 4.39 points for naive persistence over 240 backtest cases, with 80% bands covering 84% of outcomes.

For the export share toward China, the published model is random walk with drift: CRPS 3.91 points against 4.13 points for naive persistence over 240 backtest cases, with 80% bands covering 69% of outcomes.
Venezuela reports no mineral trade to UN Comtrade in the covered years, so every trade-based indicator is absent there.

Chinese official finance (AidData) ends in 2021, US finance is DFC/OPIC only, debt by creditor exists for China only, and the legislative stance comes from the text model (zero-shot baseline, not yet validated).
19 dated events are in the event list, 19 of them still in draft.

human.title: The region: China buys and lends, the United States talks, and the index records both
human.author: AI-drafted from the site's indicators; not yet reviewed by the project owner
human.text_md:
## Alignment

In 2024 the index leans most toward China in Suriname (+38), Peru (+34) and Bolivia (+31) and least in Paraguay (0) and Argentina (−13); ten of the twelve countries have an index that year, Uruguay and Venezuela do not [index_value:influence:2024]. The lean is made of two different things. In Peru, Chile, Brazil and Ecuador it is trade: around half of each country's mineral exports went to China in the latest year, against 3% to 14% to the United States [concentration:share_cn_x:2025]. In Suriname, Bolivia and Venezuela it is money: Chinese commitments that the mineral trade does not show [flow_finance:CN:2015-2021]. Documented Chinese commitments to the twelve reached US$195 bn over 2000–2021 against US$6 bn from US institutions over 1986–2024, in every sector [finance_event:CN] [finance_event:US]. The statements run the other way: US officials produce 2.2 statements for every Chinese one and nine in ten of their coded positions on China are negative [statement:count:bloc=United States] [statement:count:bloc=China]. My reading: Washington argues and Beijing lends and buys; the executives of the region praise both and sell to the buyer.

## Trajectory

Between 2019 and 2024 the Chinese index rose most in Brazil (+10.2) and Bolivia (+9.6) and fell most in Suriname (−13.2) and Argentina (−7.3) [index_value:influence:CN:2024]. Across the reporting countries in 2025, lithium (73%), iron ore (68%) and manganese (62%) are the minerals that go most to China; tin (17%), bauxite (14%) and copper (13%) go most to the United States [concentration:share_cn_x:lithium:2025] [concentration:share_us_x:copper:2025]. The panel regressions find no finance-to-trade link: Chinese commitments over the previous three years go with a slightly lower share of exports to China the next year (−1.2 points per standard deviation, wild bootstrap p 0.04), while a country one standard deviation more democratic buys 15.7 points more of its mineral imports from the United States [regression_result:exports_to_cn:twfe:finance_flow_lag1] [regression_result:imports_from_us:twfe:electoral_democracy]. The event windows, all around draft events, show the share to China rising after the Chinese export controls of 2023–2024 and after the US measures of 2017–2022, which in my reading means those measures coincided with the pull of Chinese demand and did not reverse it [event_effect:family=CN:export_control:CN] [event_effect:family=US:strategy:CN].

## Risks and likely next moves

The published models expect persistence: under the baseline China keeps about half of the exports of Peru, Chile, Brazil and Ecuador in 2030, and under the US-reshoring scenario still more than two fifths; the United States reaches a quarter only in Chile [forecast:export_share:CN:us_reshoring:2030] [forecast:export_share:US:us_reshoring:2030:CHL]. Parity in Chile, Brazil or Peru would take about US$10 bn of yearly exports switching in each, and only copper and iron ore could carry it [insights:parity_gap]. The next moves already on the record are the US–Argentina agreements of October and November 2025, Brazil's critical-minerals law of September 2026, the Section 232 copper tariff and China's suspended October 2025 controls [event:us_arg_swap_line_2025] [event:bra_lei_15506_critical_minerals] [event:cn_export_controls_oct_2025_suspended]. In my reading, the test of 2026 is whether the surge of statements (a third of the dataset is from 2026) is followed by commitments in the US finance record; if it is not, the contest stays one of words against ore.

## What would change this reading

Reviewed events that confirmed or dropped the windows above; a validated text model; a second coder on the statements; US commitments after 2024 approaching the Chinese figures; AidData's next release covering 2022–2024; or a 2026 trade year in which Chile's or Peru's US share rose by more than the scenario's two points.

speaker.name: Michael Kozak
speaker.role: Senior Bureau Official, Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs, U.S. Department of State

records.event_context: SFRC Western Hemisphere subcommittee hearing 'The National Security Strategy and the Western Hemisphere'
records.summary_en: Kozak told senators the US had signed seven cooperative critical-minerals MOUs in the hemisphere to speed resource development and was pushing US and allied firms into critical infrastructure to push out competitors; he also accused China of economic retaliation against Panama.

records.quote_en: On critical minerals, we have signed seven cooperative MOUs that will speed up resource development.

source.name: U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee (written testimony)

records.notes: Countries of the seven MOUs not named in testimony.

records.event_context: Testimony to House Appropriations Subcommittee on National Security, Department of State and Related Programs
records.summary_en: Discussing China in the Americas, Rubio said Beijing seeks access to critical minerals and mining through long-term contracts and infrastructure investments, and that countries turn to Chinese firms because they are the only ones showing up, requiring US alternatives.
records.quote_original: They try to establish for themselves access to critical minerals, mining of any sort and gain these long-term contracts
records.quote_en: They try to establish for themselves access to critical minerals, mining of any sort and gain these long-term contracts

records.event_context: Close of 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial; 11 bilateral frameworks incl. Argentina, Ecuador, Paraguay, Peru

records.quote_en: took a decisive step to reshape the global market for critical minerals and rare earths, strengthening supply chains that underpin the world's most advanced technologies

speaker.name: U.S. Department of State
speaker.role: Host of 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial (Sec. Marco Rubio)

records.event_context: 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial, Washington
records.summary_en: State Department fact sheet on the ministerial hosted by Rubio and VP Vance listed attending delegations including Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Ecuador, Paraguay and Peru, new bilateral critical minerals frameworks/MOUs with Argentina, Ecuador, Paraguay and Peru, and $565 million for rare earth extraction in Brazil.

speaker.name: Government of the People's Republic of China
speaker.role: Central government (policy paper issued via Xinhua)

records.event_context: Third China's Policy Paper on Latin America and the Caribbean
records.summary_en: China's third policy paper on LAC, under its energy and resources cooperation section, pledges full-industrial-chain energy cooperation and green development and use of mineral resources across all stages. It also proposes mechanisms for long-term supply of energy and resource products with local-currency pricing and settlement.
records.quote_original: 加强矿产资源各环节绿色开发利用
records.quote_en: Strengthen the green development and utilization of mineral resources across all links
records.notes: Section (五) 能源资源合作; full text published by Xinhua; English version referenced at english.www.gov.cn content_WS693962c3c6d00ca5f9a08069

speaker.name: The White House (Trump administration)
speaker.role: National Security Strategy of the United States

records.event_context: 2025 National Security Strategy, 'Trump Corollary' to the Monroe Doctrine
records.summary_en: The NSS says the Western Hemisphere holds strategic resources the US should develop with regional allies, orders an interagency process to identify strategic points and resources for protection and joint development, and pledges to deny non-Hemispheric competitors ownership or control of strategically vital assets.
records.quote_original: The Western Hemisphere is home to many strategic resources that America should partner with regional allies to develop
records.quote_en: The Western Hemisphere is home to many strategic resources that America should partner with regional allies to develop
records.notes: Document dated November 2025, published early December 2025; China implied as 'non-Hemispheric competitor' (stance inferred)

speaker.name: Guo Jiakun
speaker.role: Spokesperson, Ministry of Foreign Affairs of China

records.event_context: Response to SOUTHCOM commander's remarks at South American Defense Conference in Argentina
records.summary_en: Responding to the US Southern Command chief's claim in Argentina that China was infiltrating the Western Hemisphere and grabbing resources, Guo Jiakun said the US has long interfered in and sought to control Latin America and that the region is nobody's backyard.
records.quote_original: 拉美和加勒比不是谁的后院，中拉合作不针对第三方，也不应受到第三方的干扰。
records.quote_en: Latin America and the Caribbean is nobody's backyard; China-LAC cooperation does not target any third party and should not be interfered with by any third party.
records.notes: US remark referred to 'resources' generally, not a specific mineral; borderline relevance. MFA transcript not fetched.

records.event_context: Proclamation 'Adjusting Imports of Copper into the United States' (Section 232)
records.summary_en: Trump imposed a 50% Section 232 tariff on semi-finished copper products and intensive derivatives from 1 August 2025 while leaving ores, concentrates and cathodes out, citing a single foreign country's dominance of global smelting and refining.
records.quote_original: Today, a single foreign country dominates global copper smelting and refining, controlling over 50 percent of global smelting capacity
records.quote_en: Today, a single foreign country dominates global copper smelting and refining, controlling over 50 percent of global smelting capacity
records.notes: Global measure, no LatAm country named; relevant to Chile/Peru as main copper suppliers; cathode exclusion reported by CTV/Reuters https://www.ctvnews.ca/world/trumps-tariffs/article/trump-imposes-50-tariff-on-copper-imports-white-house-says/ . 'Single foreign country' implicitly China (not named).

speaker.name: China-CELAC Forum (Fourth Ministerial Meeting)
speaker.role: Joint document of China and CELAC member states

records.event_context: China-CELAC Forum Fourth Ministerial Meeting, Beijing; Joint Action Plan 2025-2027
records.summary_en: The China-CELAC Joint Action Plan 2025-2027 contains an 'Energy and resources' chapter that commits to exploring investment in energy transition and advanced energy storage and to geoscience cooperation; it names no specific minerals. Its law-enforcement section calls for exchanges on combating illegal mining and illegal trade in precious metals.
records.quote_original: 探索双方能源转型与先进储能技术合作投资机遇，助力双方共同实现能源绿色低碳转型。
records.quote_en: Explore cooperation and investment opportunities in energy transition and advanced energy storage technology, helping both sides achieve a green, low-carbon energy transition.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the PRC

records.notes: No explicit lithium/copper language; Spanish version: static.poder360.com.br/2025/05/plano-de-acao-china-latina.pdf. Joint China-CELAC text, coded as china_central_gov.
